utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all present in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, sir. Would you please be so kind as to tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, would you please tell us what your profession is. Tell us about your educational background and your career.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was a pilot in the air force of the JNA, later on the army of Yugoslavia. I graduated from the air force academy in Zadar and served in Split and Batajnica in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please tell us the makes of aircraft you flew during your career, and do you still fly or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I flew helicopters of different makes, but most often on the MI8 or HT40 helicopter. I'm currently retire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you also fly the Gazelle helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're interested in the year 1991. Can you tell us where you served in 1991 or, rather, in which unit did you fly helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I served at the Batajnica airport in the 890th Mixed Helicopter Squadron, and I flew a HT40.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just intervene in the transcript -- oh, now it's fine. It's the 890th Mixed Helicopter Squadron. Was your unit assigned a mission relative to the transport from the Vukovar battlefield?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Among other missions, the unit also had the mission to transport medical corps or, rather, the -- for the purposes of the medical corps of the Motorised Brigade. Our mission specifically was to transport the wounded from the Vukovar battlefield or, more precisely, from Negoslavci where the hospital was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you've mentioned the transport of the wounded, you can you tell us what the capacity of the HT40 helicopter you flew was, specifically when it comes to the transporting of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The HT40 helicopter could hold approximately 15 to 16 slightly wounded, that is to say those who are able to stay seated, or 12 wounded on stretchers. Those were the maximum capacities of the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were the services of your helicopter squadron requested in advance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Depending on the situation, one HT40 helicopter that was set aside for the transporting of the wounded was located in the village of Negoslavci. In the event of greater needs, our other helicopters that were stationed at Batajnica were requested to fly in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to your helicopter at the Negoslavci heliodrom -- heliport, were there any other helicopters to be found there on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one Gazelle helicopter for the purposes of the command and for the purposes of transporting wounded from the temporary hospital at Negoslavci to the VMA, that is to say the Military Medical Academy. If one single wounded had to be transported.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who made up the crew of the HT40 helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The crew of the HT40 helicopter was made up of two pilots and one mechanic. Thus three members of the crew in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you were assigned missions to transport a group of wounded, who assigned such missions to you? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We received direct orders from the superior commander. The crew at Negoslavci received their orders from the air force commander attached to the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the crew stationed at Negoslavci. Were there shifts of crews or was there just this one single crew?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: There were shifts of crews that rotated every three to four days. The crews would change depending on the availability of manpower and the circumstances dictated by the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you ever transport the commander of the Guards Brigade, Colonel Mrksic, in a HT40 helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he, during his stay at Negoslavci, ever used that make of helicopter for his purposes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please be shown Exhibit 765, which is the flight log of the 890th Transport Helicopter Squadron for HT40 helicopters. Yesterday, we provided copies of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have this flight log before you? Can you tell me is this the log of your squadron for the make of the helicopter you flew in 1991 in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether important data about the crews and sorties of the helicopters in the relevant period were entered into this log.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The main data contained in flight schedules were entered into the log; that is to say, the time of flight that was carried out, names of the passengers, the crew, the number of the helicopter which flew, and the numerical code of the exercise in order to avoid writing details about it. Let us say that it was a sort of a code used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This document which is kept for a long time and is in effect the document on the basis of which the number of hours flown is determined for a particular aircraft, as well as the persons who flew the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, both for the aircraft itself and the crew. After the data is entered into the flight log, the members of the crew enter the same data into their own respective records about the details of the flight. The data are subsequently confirmed by the superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the relevant period, what was your position in the squadron? Were you just a helicopter pilot or did you have a post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the helicopter squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please look at the entry for the 21st of November, 1991, in this flight log, which is page 1D040047 in the B/C/S. And in the English version that's page 1D040063. Do you see the entry for the sortie which was carried out between 8.00 and 9.35? Did your view fly this sortie?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was the head of the crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the route of this flight; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We took off from the Batajnica airport to the football pitch in the village of Negoslavci, whereupon we flew over to the VMA heliport, that is to say the heliport of the Military Medical Academy, and returned to the Batajnica airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You've told us already but I will ask you again. On this flight and on that day, did you transport Colonel Mrksic in the helicopter that you yourself flew?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: As I've already answered you, no, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know Colonel Mrksic from before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to know him or how far you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: We met in the village of Negoslavci, and I knew him as the commander of the Guards Brigade since, for a period of time, I was stationed in the village of Negoslavci as the reserve crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if at the time you took off from Negoslavci on that day, when you took off from Negoslavci to Belgrade, was there another helicopter that took off from the heliport at the football pitch you mentioned at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: At the time I was there, no, it did not. There was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No questions from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you given evidence before in a court?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When was that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: A long, long time ago. It must have been ten years ago, possibly more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In this court, we are given a document. Can you just look at me for a moment, please? Thank you. We're given a document with your name, your date of birth, and the evidence, we're told the evidence that you're going to give. Now, when did you first speak to the lawyers of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The first time, I don't know. It was last year, up to a year. I can't remember specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when did you arrive here in The Hague for this trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of September this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just read out what your summary says. It gives your date of birth. It indicates that you're an ML -- or a MI8 helicopter. "On the 21st of November, 1991, in the morning hours, around 8.00, the witness, together with his co-pilot, transported Major Tesic, Vujovic, and two wounded persons from Negoslavci to Belgrade. He will testify that Colonel Mrksic never used the MI8 helicopters but exclusively Gazelles." Do you remember taking a man named Miroljub Vujovic on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, you see, he's given evidence at the military court in Belgrade in 2001 that he actually went by helicopter on the morning of the 21st from Negoslavci to Belgrade, and clearly it had to be your helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That is possible. I'm not saying that it wasn't the case. However, I don't know the man, and I simply can't confirm that he was in that helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one objection to raise, which stems from what has so far been the established practice used by Mr. Moore. We can't confront a witness with his own statement and then ask him what he thinks about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic, I don't know the real point of that objection. This is cross-examination, not examination-in-chief, and in cross-examination, if there was a difficulty or a difference between a statement in the evidence, it would properly be put to the witness. But what is being done here is not putting a statement but a summary provided to the Prosecution, which is -- may or may not be something the witness has seen, and he's being asked about the reliability of that statement or whether he himself here remembers certain things in it, and it doesn't seem to me that that's objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're very generous, Mr. Vasic, this morning. Let us both continue in that spirit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That gentleman, when he gave evidence, said that he travelled with Colonel Mrksic and Major Tesic. Now, can you explain how that might be? And before you answer, in fairness to you, Colonel Mrksic, on two occasions, indicated that he had travelled in the morning, and that on one of those occasions -- and I say one of those occasions, he said he also travelled by helicopter when he was on his way to Belgrade for the special meeting. Now, can you explain that, how it is you say that Mrksic didn't travel and Mrksic himself said he did travel and also another passenger who you accept travelled, how he said that Mrksic was on that helicopter? Is it a case you might have forgotten?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I think in fairness to the position, it should be added to your preliminary comments that evidence about how Colonel Mrksic travelled has varied, but as you have said, he himself has given evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might it be that with the passage of time you have simply forgotten? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No. If I may just explain. My evidence was that Colonel Mrksic did not fly in my helicopter at all, the one that I flew, the HT40. Whether he ever flew with a different crew in that same helicopter, or perhaps he used a Gazelle, is not something that I can say. One thing I do know for certain is Colonel Mrksic never flew in any of my helicopters, not then, not later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at some of the documents that we have. You will have a bundle. It's Exhibit, I think, 764. I hope I've got my numbers right. It relates, I hope, to the Gazelle helicopter. Now, have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just see if my English translation corresponds with your -- your B/C/S original document. Can we just have a small exercise. Can we look at the 19th of November. The pilots should be Minic and Nikolic. Have you got that? Have you got it in front of you? You have documents there.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No, not now. That's not what it says. I just have the title page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, with a bit of luck we'll soon get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are there hard copies for the witness, or does it have to be always e-court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just check? 19th of November, H45, 892, Minic, Nikolic. Is that right? Then it's number 300, BT-Kovin, and then 1535 takeoff, 1600 landing. Have you got that in front you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Does this apply to the Gazelle helicopter that normally was based at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: This applies to a Gazelle. However, based on what I see on my monitor, the helicopter was stationed at Batajnica, because that's what BT stands for, and it was on its way to Kovin airport. In this other column you can see that it returned at 1700 hours from Kovin to Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's just look at this -- this flight log, because this document relates to one helicopter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, then you explain to me, please, what the 19th and the 21st, how you can distinguish between the helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The first column contains the type of helicopter. H45 stands for a Gazelle. 892, for example, is the helicopter's military number, its proper name in the army, if I may put it that way. Another helicopter of that same make bears a different number, and these numbers are used to distinguish individual helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if we're looking at the 19th of November by way of example, we've got the Gazelle, which is H45. We've got what I will call the identification number of the helicopter, which is 892, and we've got this helicopter travelling from Minic -- flown by Minic and Nikolic. It's going from BT to Kovin, and then it's returning from Kovin to BT. So that is one helicopter flight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's right. No. These are two flights; one to Kovin and one back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So let's look, then, at helicopter 892, shall we? So 892, on the 19th of November, flies into BT. You agree with that, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The 19th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The next time it makes a flight is on the 21st of November. We can see that. And it goes BT, Top, and then Top to Negoslavci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I assume it to be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just deal, then, with the larger helicopter, the one that you were flying. Its capacity, clearly, could carry four passengers. You said 15, 16, depending on who was wounded or not. And you have told us about passengers. How many passengers were flying with that large helicopter on the morning of the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I can't remember based on the log, but I assume that information entered here is accurate. It would seem to indicate four passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how do you get four passengers from this particular document? Can you tell us? Explain.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I think I could explain. I could show you what I have here. This is a flight log, and it looks like this in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: So what that means is -- there is the continuation on the other page. It says "flight" and "flight time," and then the designation L in column 19. That means flights, which means three flights. And then P, these are passengers, four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what does M stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It means materiel, cargo, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when you tell us that you can't remember based on the log how many passengers, you assume that the -- that you assume that the information entered here is accurate. It's not a case of you actually remembering. It's a case of you refreshing your memory from this document; i.e., four passengers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I look at this document and it tells me that there were four passengers. I can't remember if that was actually the case or not, but there is absolutely no reason for the information that was entered here to be inaccurate. This was written on the very same day that the flight was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could Your Honour forgive me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it's not a case of names of passengers. It's a case of numbers of passengers. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a couple of questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you first explain what these flights mean that are recorded in the log? What does this concept imply, "flights"? I see here that on the 21st of November you had three flights, or so you say.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: When one says "flights," that implies the time between the time a helicopter first takes off and the time it touches ground again. So, for example, if I made a flight from Batajnica to Negoslavci on this day, that is one flight. Then from Negoslavci to the Military Medical Academy, that was the other flight. And then from the hospital back to Batajnica was the third flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you landed at the VMA, Military Medical Academy airport. Did you only land there if you were ferrying the wounded? Was that the only reason you ever landed there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we say based on that that on the 21st of November you were ferrying some wounded persons again, because you say you landed at the VMA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: For the most part, HT40 was used for ferrying wounded, and all the missions carried out at the time were for that purpose, which does not mean in itself that no one else was ever ferried. In addition to wounded people, there were officers being ferried, too, who used the occasional flight to get to Belgrade, or back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience as a pilot, can you tell us if brigade commanders, army commanders, corps commanders used their own helicopter on their missions, or would they normally fly together with wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to that question. This is case specific. It relates to a flight to Belgrade, and all this is speculation in relation to conduct either before or after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we see that as going to weight, not admissibility. Carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat the question? I've been thrown slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your experience as a pilot, and you did fly brigade commanders as well as even those of a higher rank. When they went on a mission, would they go in their own helicopter, the one that was assigned to them, or were they use the helicopter, the same helicopters that were used for ferrying wounded or equipment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: In principle, if there was just a single person escorting them, they would take a Gazelle. If it was a larger group travelling, and only in that case, they would use a larger helicopter. But if there was a one-man escort only, then they would normally use a Gazelle, the smaller helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A Gazelle has what seating capacity exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I flew that helicopter, too, so I'm somewhat familiar with it. It can take up to two crew and three passengers, the pilot, the mechanic, and a maximum of three passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible for an aircraft like that to take only one pilot and four other passengers? Would that be in line with the regulations?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, as long as the final destination is an airport, and as long as there is a crew awaiting its landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you took off on this mission on the 21st of November, can you remember whether over at Negoslavci, at the heliport in Negoslavci, there was a Gazelle that was in theory available to be used?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I can't say with sure and certain knowledge that there was one there, but as far as I remember, there was both a MI8 and a Gazelle, but I can't be positive about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Babic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder whether you can help the Chamber with a couple of matters, please. Firstly, the H40, that was your medium, heavy transport helicopter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's right. HT40 is the medium transport helicopter. Depending on the exact type, because sometimes you can remove certain parts inside the helicopter, and then in that case it can take up to 24 passengers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the maker of that aircraft; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was of Russian make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the maker?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did it have a name that was typically used for it? What did you call it, the HT40 or some other typical name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Russian name is MI8. We called it HT, which stands for transport helicopter, and then the number assigned to it is 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. The Gazelle is the H45; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's one type of Gazelle. There are several versions, as it were. The air force at the time had another type of Gazelle which was called H42. The appearance of the helicopter was identical to the other one, but the engine was somewhat less powerful. That was the only difference, and all the other features were the same. And the helicopter was also -- this other type was also referred to as a Gazelle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And who was -- or which company made the Gazelle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: It is a French helicopter. A Mostar-based company called Soko in the former Yugoslavia also produced those. Most of the Gazelles used by the air force, by the Yugoslav air force I expect were produced in the Soko Mostar company that produced helicopters and aeroplanes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The flight log that you've been looking at for the Gazelle, Exhibit 764, shows both H42 and H45. So that's a flight log covering both types of Gazelle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Because to all practical intents, these were the same helicopter with a different designation, and the difference in terms of the engine power was very slight. But one of these was called H42, and the other was referred to as H45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this flight log is the log of the 890 Squadron; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. The reason being the 890 Squadron had a number of different helicopter types.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could turn to the log for the Gazelle for flights on the 21st of November. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that shows flights by two H45s, one number 893 and the other number 892, on the 21st of November. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Number H -- number 892 appears to have been flown at 0800 for 40 minutes from Batajnica to Topcider and then to Negoslavci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Topcider, as I understand it, is in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the Batajnica airport is in the Belgrade area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: The Batajnica airport is roughly 20 kilometres away from Belgrade to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And there was no other flight for 892 on the 21st of November, according to this log; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you look now at the next day, the 22nd of November. Aircraft 892 is shown again as having three flights where one of them was aborted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mission was aborted. They took off, and for some reason they landed and the mission was aborted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first flight appears to be that which is first there at 0800. The pilot was Milosevic, and Nikolic as co-pilot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Nikolic was a mechanic, because the helicopter of the Gazelle make only -- is only flown by one pilot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that flight from Batajnica to Dedinje?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the aborted mission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, the 0800, first flight of the day on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: That was a flight from Batajnica to Dedinje. That's what transpires from the log.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What interests the Chamber is how the aircraft got from Negoslavci on the 21st of November, at the end of its last flight, to Batajnica at the beginning of its first flight on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't help you there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would appear that there must have been a flight that is not recorded in the log; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC
utterances.text: Or possibly an error occurred in the entering of the data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Is there anything further, Mr. Vasic, arising from that that you want to mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the next witness will be more pertinent to answer the question. That's Nenad Novicevic, and I will use that opportunity when he takes the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Sir, you'll be pleased to know that completes the end of your questioning. The Chamber is grateful for your assistance and for your attendance here, and you are now free to return to your ordinary life. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the next witness is coming, Mr. Vasic, it's been pointed out to me there's a transcript error in my question at page 18, line 25. The question was that it is not reported in the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was indeed the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while we're waiting for the next witness, the Defence for the accused Miroslav Radic would like to clarify a matter that was raised yesterday, namely the release of Mr. Radic from the obligation to keep a military secret. Mr. Moore referred to that yesterday, and you said that we should in our communication, mutual communication, address the matter. I wish to inform you and my learned friends from the OTP that all the witnesses, the four witnesses for the accused Radic, were released from the obligation to keep the military secret. The date is the 7th of September. We received that information, and we have to state that we feel quite uncomfortable with the fact that certain matters are being raised before the Trial Chamber before other channels are used to verify some information necessary for the parties. We believe it would be necessary to first double-check the information received before it is presented with the -- presented to the Trial Chamber, which results then in an unpleasant situation for the Defence teams. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, quite a different matter before the next witness comes in. I have the obligation to inform the Trial Chamber of something, but could we first move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If the witness would sit down for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please stand and read aloud the affirmation on the card.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Nenad Novicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell us, during your service in the JNA, which schools did you graduate from, and which positions did you hold?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the air force academy. Upon completion of my education, I was flight teacher at a schooling centre, whereupon I became part of the squadron for reconnaissance, and as of 1989, I was a member of the transport squadron in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell us which squadron were you a member of as of 1989? Does it have its title or number?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That was the 890th Transport Mixed Squadron within the 138th Transport Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said mixed squadron. What does that mean? Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: This means that it had two squads of transport helicopters, MI8 and one squad of light reconnaissance or transport helicopters of the make Gazelle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this one squad of light transport helicopters of the Gazelle type. Can you tell us which types of helicopters were part of the squad at the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the squad of Gazelle helicopters have several different types of helicopters in terms of the power engine?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Now I understand. There were two types, SA341 and SA342. One of them had 600 horsepower and the other one had 900 horsepower.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 764. That's the flight log of the 80th [as interpreted] Transport Squadron for the Gazelle make of helicopters. Do you have that before you? Could we have, please, page 1D040080 in the B/C/S, and in English 1D040086. Beneath the term "squadron" it says H42/45. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: H42 is the military code for SA341 Gazelle, whereas the H45 is the military code for the SA342 helicopter, which is the one which has 900 horsepower.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that this flight log contains data for both types of Gazelle helicopters?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during your career as a pilot, which helicopters did you fly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: If you're referring to H42 and H45, I flew both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're interested in the year 1991. Which unit did you fly in in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: In the 890th Transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Which type of helicopters did you fly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: HT42 and HT45.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're interested in the events at the Vukovar battlefield in 1991. Was your squadron given a mission relative to the Vukovar battlefield and, in particular, related to the needs of the Motorised Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We provided air support to the Motorised Guards Brigade in terms of transporting commanding officers and wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which helicopters were used for the task of providing transport support to the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: All types of helicopters that were flown in the squadron, and that means MI8 and the Gazelle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many aircraft were at the disposal of the Guards Motorised Brigade for the -- these purposes?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that exactly. I do know that in the place of Negoslavci at the pitch there in Vukovar we always had one MI8 and one Gazelle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you flew the Gazelle helicopter of -- and more precisely you flew both types of the Gazelle helicopter, can you tell us for what purposes this type of helicopter was used in Negoslavci in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The Gazelle was used for transporting commanders, officers, and for any urgent cases of transportation of wounded over to the Military Medical Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the wounded were transported, was it necessary to effect some changes in the Gazelle helicopter, or could it just fly in its original condition?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The Gazelle helicopter is a light helicopter for transporting passengers and wounded. Where the wounded were transported, certain preparations had to be made, and these included the removal of the left seat of the co-pilot, the removal of the back seat in order to place a stretcher there. In such condition, the helicopter could hold one wounded person, one person escorting the wounded person, and a pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the commander of the Guards Motorised Brigade used this type of helicopter only whenever he needed the services of his squadron? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that he flew on the Gazelle, and I personally flew the aircraft when he was on several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The pilots of this Gazelle helicopters, what was the practice? How was their stay regulated? Did they stay throughout at Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Vukovar operation lasted roughly two months. We rotated every seven to eight days. The crews would rotate. The duty days would be around seven days, and at that time we would be put up with the command of the Guards Brigade at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there strictly regulated rotations in terms of the number of days, or could they vary depending on the flight schedule you had?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. This was not strictly regulated. It could be further apart or closer in terms of rotations. There were four or five of us in all, and we rotated according to how we saw fit. And when I say "how we saw fit," we also had to coordinate our work with our families, and we tried to accommodate each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to what is contained in Exhibit 764, the flight log. What sort of a document is a flight log, please, in the briefest of terms?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The flight log records the activity of a squadron on a given day. It contains the members of the crew, helicopter type, time of takeoff, time of landing, duration of flight, the conditions under which the flight was carried out, was it at night or during daytime, number of passengers, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know who entered the data into the flight log?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The flight log is a document kept by the squadron command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I presume that the commander or an officer designated by the commander is duty-bound to enter data into the log.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander has an assistant who is tasked with that precise duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do the pilots themselves enter the information on the flights carried out in some sort of a document?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Pilots enter data into a flight schedule. The squadron commander assigns a mission through the flight schedule. And in view of the fact that these missions are sometimes completed in the course of the day and sometimes only on the following day, upon their return from the flight pilots enter information on all these different elements into the flight schedule, which had earlier been drafted in the form of an order, which data are later entered into an operational flight log of the squadron.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is that the flight log that we have in front of us, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that pilots when back from a mission enter the relevant information, the relevant flight information. What about those who were on duty in Negoslavci for a couple of days? Do they enter the same sort of information into the logbook once everything has been carried out?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Having returned from a mission, they report to their squadron commander about their flights, the destination, the duration, and the number of passengers ferried.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this information is entered into the flight schedule, the flight schedule that you told us about, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you say that there's a person who is in charge of entering information into this log containing all the exact times, and then they would copy information from the flight schedule and enter this information into the flight log. Is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now for something that the Chamber has dealt with with the previous witness, but I think you are probably the best placed person to explain about the identification numbers pertaining to the helicopters mentioned in this log. Can you please have a look at the log, sir. Specifically the date is the 18th, the 19th, the 21st, the 22nd, and the 24th of November. That is 1D0483 in the B/C/S and 0489 in the English. And the exhibit number is 764. Do you have that page in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Among other information entered are the ID numbers of helicopters carrying out certain missions. We see that information recorded in column two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There's something there that I believe might need clarifying. On the 18th of November, if you can have a look, please, the following crew: Pantovic and Marceta. Can you tell us the ID for that helicopter and its destination for this particular flight?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The ID number is 893, the drill number is 61, the route being Batajnica, Banjica, Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This was the last flight on that day, at least according to the log, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next date appears to be the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So according to this, the helicopter should be in Negoslavci, the 893, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the following entry where this helicopter is mentioned. The number is -- the date is the 21st of November, 1991. Is that right? Can you read the entry for us, please, with the helicopter ID number? I'm talking about the 20th of November. Can you tell us what the crew was and the destination?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: You probably mean the 21st, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: HT45, 893, Pantovic, Marceta, Negoslavci-Banjica-Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There are no other flights entered for that day after this one, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That appears to be the last flight on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the helicopter should now be at Batajnica. That's what the document indicates, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What it says in relation to 893, its location after 12.20 should be Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And now the next entry in relation to the 893. That is on the 24th of November, 1991. 9.10 is the time. Can you please have a look? I think you actually flew this helicopter. Can you tell us what the crew was and the destination?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Novicevic, Bajic, the number is 893, Negoslavci-Mladenovo, takeoff 9.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 24th of November is when this helicopter left Negoslavci and flew to Mladenovo, and you were the pilot, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we can just please go back to the previous entry on the 21st of November where we established that the helicopter was supposed in Batajnica, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Not in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll clarify later how that came to pass. Let's now go to 892, the other helicopter that is logged on this page and follow its movements. Let's start with the 19th of November, 1991. The entry in relation to 892, helicopter 892, please read that out for us. What was its route? I see it made two flights on that day?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: On that day the 892 took off at 1535, the crew being Minic, Nikolic, the route being Batajnica-Kovin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the same helicopter on the same day? Did it make another flight?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. At 1700 hours it left Kovin and returned to Batajnica with the same crew Minic, Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So at the end of that day the 19th of November, the 892 was supposed to be at Batajnica, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The next entry in relation to that helicopter is on the 21st of November, 1991. I see that you were one of the crew. Can you please read the crew and the destination for us?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: 21st of November, the 892, Novicevic, Bajic, the route was Batajnica-Topcider-Negoslavci, takeoff at 0800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So placed on this it seems that the helicopter had been left at Batajnica on the 19th the -- two days before. You took off in that helicopter and you landed in Negoslavci, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's particular it a step further with this helicopter, and I am I'm talking about the following day, the 22nd of November, 1991. Please read the entry in relation to that helicopter's takeoff on the 21st of November. What is the crew and what is the destination?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: 22nd of November, 892, Milosevic, Nikolic, Batajnica-Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on the previous entry that helicopter should be at Negoslavci not at Batajnica. Wouldn't that seem to be the case?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if this is a convenient time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novicevic, let us now go back to the flight log, Exhibit 764, more specifically the page containing the entries for the 18th and the 24th of November. We've look at the chronology for the 893 and the 892. I think the only day they overlap is the 21st of November, 1991. Based on the logbook, where is the 892 supposed to be after the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The 892, after the 21st, should be at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the 893?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the entry for the 21st of November, the 893 should be at Batajnica. However, that wasn't the case. There probably was an error when recording this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to this area later on. The 892 was supposed to be at Negoslavci. Where does it take off from the next time it does? Can you find that in the log, please?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I can. The 892 takes off on the 22nd of November from Batajnica and is en route for Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There seems to be a discrepancy there. Instead of Negoslavci it takes off from Batajnica, does it not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the 893 at the end of the 21st? It's supposed to be at Batajnica, isn't it? Can you tell us where it took off from next, the 893, the next time it flew?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The next flight of the 893 was on the 24th of November, on the Negoslavci-Mladenovo route, and I was the pilot for that flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the error consists in the fact that the recording indicates that the aircraft was supposed to be in Batajnica, whereas you actually took off from Negoslavci. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So what actually constitutes this error? Is this something you can spot?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: This is probably when happened: Mr. Pantovic, who was at Negoslavci on the 21st of November with the 893, and I, who landed on the 892, we exchanged our places in Negoslavci on that day. So Mr. Pantovic was off to Belgrade on the 892 instead. When the flight schedule was being drawn up, as he was supposed to be on the 893, he drew a thick red line here, and whoever entered the relevant timing recorded Pantovic as being on the 893.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So what that means is that Pantovic was off to Belgrade on the 892, and the 893 remained in Negoslavci. Is that what you're suggesting?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Things being what they are, how would this have worked? Would that imply that there was a lack of logic or precision in relation to the flights that followed over the following days, or would everything be all right on the 21st, for example, if we had the 893 instead of the 892 and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Actually, the timings for the 21st should say 892 in both cases, the flight log. Pantovic, Marceta, 892, and Novicevic, Bajic 892 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The day you landed in the 892, Pantovic took the same helicopter and flew to Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may just add something. So before the -- such takeoffs, the commander would orally tell us if we were to return a helicopter or if a helicopter was supposed to stay where it was. So the helicopter that is in Vukovar stays, just by way of an example, and Pantovic goes back on the same helicopter that I had come in on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain along these same lines. So Pantovic was off in the 892. Where does that helicopter take off from the next time around for its next flight?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That is on the 22nd of November. The 892 goes Batajnica-Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The pilot being?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Milosevic. And the mechanic was Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Pantovic brought the helicopter to Batajnica, but the next person flying the helicopter was Milosevic. Was this a change of shift? How did this come about that the crew changed in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: It's very simple. On the 22nd of November, the helicopter landed at Batajnica at 12.20. The next day, on the 22nd of November, Milosevic was in charge of the mission. He went to Dedinje and then back to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think there must be an error in the transcript. 35, line 3, it should be the 22nd of November that the helicopter landed at Batajnica. Were you at the heliport when pilot Pantovic took this helicopter away, the one which you say you had flown in on?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was usual practice for us to see each other off.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you say usual practice seeing each other off, who do you mean and in what cases specifically?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: When there was a change in shift, the arriving pilot would see off the one who was due to take off and go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did Pantovic have any assistants on that flight? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I think there was a total of four men on that flight, four passengers. A total of four, I mean. A total of four persons. The mechanic plus two passengers and the pilot. I think there was a lady with them and a gentleman wearing a uniform. The reason I rather that is that it wasn't very often that ladies were flown.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: According to the log, when was this flight made, what time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when Pantovic is on his way back to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It took off at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What is recorded in the log, does that tally with how you remember this to have occurred; namely, that he took off around this time, the time recorded here, given the time of your arrival in Negoslavci on that same day and the time you spent there?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to remember specifically but just by looking at these documents I know that the documents that were kept were accurate. So a pilot's report was always accurately recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Colonel Mrksic at the time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at the heliport or inside the helicopter flown by Pantovic on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look right next to the entry for the 21st of November where your name is mentioned, you say that your name was also mentioned in relation to the 24th of November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where you went on at that day, where you flew to, and who was on board?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. We flew with Mr. Mrksic to Mladenovo, and we stayed there until half past 2.00. The headquarters was at Mladenovo. I think there was a meeting with the commander-in-chief. I didn't attend the meeting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say commander-in-chief, you mean the 1st Military District, right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Novicevic. Just another thing. This helicopter ID number, is that reflected in any other type of document in relation to helicopters that made certain flights except for this flight log? Can you find that ID number anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: You can find it in the daily flight schedule in relation to that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long is that document kept for?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: The flight plan, I don't know exactly how long it's kept for, especially at the time. This was the JNA. Regulations have changed since.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But what I would like to know is is this sort of document also kept for a hundred years, like the other one, but it appears not to be the case, is it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I think flight schedules were kept from six months up to a year. The log would normally be kept for ten years in the records of the Yugoslav air force. That's how I remember it to be, but that doesn't necessarily have to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Novicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. I've tried to clarify the matter that you had previously raised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just clarify? You have really two missing flights on the documents. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Two flights? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to go through it all again, but 892 and 893, for example, if one looks at the 893 on the 21st of November, we have got Pantovic, and the helicopter should be staying at BT, but the next movement actually is on the 24th of November. It's not from BT. It's from Negoslavci. Isn't that right? For the 893.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- that's what I'm trying to suggest. And the 892, there is a missing flight. When we look at the 21st of November, we've got Novicevic, yourself, coming into Negoslavci. And when we look at the 892, we can see on the 22nd of November it's not at Negoslavci, it's at BT. So what I'm suggesting to you, that there are two missing flights on these documents. Really a perfectly simple point. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I see it slightly differently. I just explained a while ago that the person who kept the document must have been confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we'll deal with the confusion in a minute, but am I right in saying that there's two missing flights on the documents? I mean, it's indisputable, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what to say. Based on what is written here, I can tell you that all things are in order. Pantovic went back on the helicopter on which I flew in on the 21st. If you take that bit into account, everything else comes -- falls into place. It's logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's not what I've asked. I've asked a perfectly simple question, and I'd suggest you're deliberately avoiding it. On the documents there are two missing flights. There is the not explained 21st of November arrival of the 892 at Negoslavci, and the next time it flies it don't fly from Negoslavci, it flies from BT. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I think it's right to say that you used the phrase -- that you used the phrase, when asked to clarify, "This is probably what happened." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember saying that. I have to tell you that on the basis of this document -- well, first of all, I did not draft this document. I flew into Negoslavci on the helicopter on the 21st, and my next flight was on the 24th from Negoslavci. That's as much as I know. Now, about the 892 that flew from Negoslavci to Batajnica, I didn't know other missions, because the squadron commander does not give missions to all the crews collectively. They are given their missions individually, and I don't know what other crews' missions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Please understand I am not criticising you, and I'm not trying to catch you out. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm simply saying is that when you use the phrase "this is probably what happened," you actually don't know. You are trying to estimate as best you can.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking from my memory of how these things were done, how the documentation was produced in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And I think you've told us it's very difficult to remember specifically, but that a pilot report is always accurate.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Before we take off, we enter the time, and as soon as we land we also enter the time into our notebook, and subsequently this information is conveyed to the squadron commander. It's as simple as that. All the pilots do that, and all of them have to take care of their times of flight, of their fuel and other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the reality is you don't actually know what happened.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: In what respect? Happened -- what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In why this document has the discrepancies it has, because you didn't compile it.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The document is filled out by the squadron headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you use the phrase "this is probably what happened," it is not from your knowledge, it is what you believe what happened, your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My learned friend was quite brief, and I will try to do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Novicevic, you explained to us that when you flew into Negoslavci on the 21st of November, 1991, at 8.40, having taken off at 8.00, and that the next flight was on the 24th of November at 9.10 from Negoslavci. How would you know that a colleague of yours had flown in the aircraft in the period between 21st and 24th, the one that you would use to take off? You would know that, wouldn't you, that someone had flown it in?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I was objecting to the question. It is merely a repeat of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Carry on, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you were perhaps unaware of what happened with the flight log because that was within the purview of the squadron headquarters, but you knew what was going on at the heliport at Negoslavci, that the helicopter that you used to take off for Mladenovo with Colonel Mrksic on the 24th had all the while been at the heliport in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I quite agree, Mr. Moore. How can you put that, Mr. Vasic, in re-examination? You are working out now your theory, which is not the subject of any evidence so far from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps very carefully and seeing what he said. Instead you've given all your theory and your answers in your question, and he only has to say yes. That's not good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. I will be more careful in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it means that his answer isn't really going to help anybody now on that question. That's the obvious penalty, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novicevic, do you know, do you remember who it was who gave you the mission to fly over to Mladenovo on the 24th of November, 1991, from Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I could only have been given the mission from my commander, squad commander, Mr. Minic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In giving you this assignment, did Mr. Minic give you certain guidelines in terms of the time, place, and aircraft to be used?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object. I object to this question. I object on two bases. One, it's leading; and two, it doesn't arise out of cross-examination. There was no cross-examination on this topic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, do you seek to justify the question as arising out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this arises from cross-examination because it has to do with the aircraft highlighted by my learned friend Moore in his cross-examination where he claimed that there was one flight missing, the flight involving this particular aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that was all led very specifically by you in your evidence-in-chief, and you didn't go to ask this sort of question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because I thought that the witness explained the situation in the examination-in-chief. I will, however, put a very simple question to him, and I believe that will suffice to clarify the situation without going into details about flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Novicevic, how long have you been a pilot for?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I have been flying since 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The -- how much do you know about the keeping of the documentation underlying these flights in your capacity as an experienced pilot?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Periodically I performed the duties of squad commander whenever Mr. Minic was absent. I stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for us what sort of situation would involve the loss or discrepancy in flight documentation such as the one that my learned friend alluded to?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That was impossible. It could only have happened after the bombing in 1999, and only if such documentation burnt out or burnt through for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal records, other than this it official log, of your flights in the period we've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean you do not maintain pilot's logbook?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: I do maintain my logbook, and up until 1997 I had a military logbook. Since 1997 I have been engaged in civilian flights, and I have been keeping a different logbook, because it was at that point that I left the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that your military logbook remained with the military, or do you still have it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: There is one military logbook which is the flight record and record of flights carried out, the military booklet of flights that were carried out; whereas this other flight booklet remained with the headquarters, the military headquarters after I left the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you have not been able to check your flights on the 21st of November and either side of that in any record other than this logbook which we have in front us; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I could have checked that in my flight booklet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you've not done so?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean I haven't done so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have -- you say you could have checked it. Have you done so?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, and it tallies with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you also look at Exhibit 764, the flights on the 22nd of November. They're all flights of helicopter 892; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first flight at 0800 hours was from Batajnica to Dedinje.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next flight was aborted.

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The third flight commenced at Batajnica. Does the log reveal how the aircraft got from Dedinje to Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This log is used not only for mission but also for total flight time recording; is that correct? For the maintenance of the aircraft?

utterances.speaker: NENAD NOVICEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much then. You'll be pleased to know that that completes the questioning of you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and the assistance you've been able to give, and you're now free, of course, to return to your ordinary activities. So thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we appear to have reached the time of which Mr. Domazet gave us some warning. We need to wait until Thursday for the next witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Evidently what Mr. Domazet told you and me, we will have to wait until Thursday, especially in light of what Mr. Lukic told us about Mr. Jaksic. I believe Mr. Jaksic will be an interesting witness for all those present in the courtroom, and the waiting period will not be in vain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, lifting our interest and excitement, Mr. Vasic. Now, can we deal with two other matters as we have some time. First, Mr. Moore, is there anything you would want to submit in response to Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, and three other matters in addition to -- four other matters in addition. With regard to Ms. Tapuskovic, I've been informed now by the team on behalf of Mr. Radic that the application for the four waivers was made. Our information - and we've not only double-checked we've actually triple-checked - from Serbia was that they had only received three. I accept the word of my learned friends. They say it's four and that they've received now signed notification in respect of that, that apparently being dated the 7th of September. I think that's the date. So I'm operating on the basis that they have seen those waivers and they are signed. So that matter, I think, hopefully now falls away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, could you just pause and I'll check. Is that resolving your concern, Ms. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This fully resolves our conflict if we can term it that or, rather, the misunderstanding that arose between the parties as to whether a waiver was obtained for the four witnesses. That was in fact obtained on the 7th, which takes care of our problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. May I deal with some other housekeeping matters that refers to my learned friends? If I -- thank you very much. With regard to the case of Mr. Mrksic, that is going a little quicker than had been anticipated, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would put it that it's on timetable at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour knows how bad I am on time. But in any event, there is a military expert's report to be served. From memory and having spoken to my learned friend, I think it was to be served by the 18th of September. Given the proposed timetable, it may well be that the case for Mr. Mrksic will finish earlier than they had originally believed and we had anticipated. What concerns us is clearly if it is an expert's report, we should have an appropriate time to receive it and look at it and reply if necessary, and the 18th perhaps puts it very tight to the wire, if I may use that phrase, when it comes to the calling of that witness. I would firstly ask the following question: Whether there is a report in being that could be served now, which would then remove the difficulties on time or certainly diminish them. That would be the first submission that I make in relation to that topic. May I move on to the other topics. With regard to the 002 diary, I have been asked by my learned friends on behalf of Mr. Radic if they could see the original document, which of course they are perfectly entitled to do so. I think it's right to say that there is a desire for an expert to look at it.
