If that is the case, we would clearly wish to have our own expert look at it, and from my own experience, though not as widespread as the Court's, it is probably desirable if the two experts look at it simultaneously. If there are any samples of handwriting that are required, they should be done with the experts present. I for my part am quite prepared for the diary to be taken to Belgrade or any other location that my learned friends deem to be appropriate. The difficulty is the liaising of the experts. I received that information this morning, and we are now taking steps to ensure that that is done expeditiously. I don't know what the third step will be. It may well be as a result of some findings that an application will be made to the Court, but I'm not going to put the cart before the horse in relation to that. So with regard to the diary, the answer is the Prosecution are willing to facilitate my learned friends. We need experts, and it's really a question of a timetable and location. So perhaps if my learned friends could assist on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we talked to the OTP as you had ordered. We believe that the war diary or note is an important document. We only got it once the cross-examination of that witness had been completed. We have noticed a number of things that indicate that there is a need for a handwriting expert to have a look, and the OTP agrees. I think the two experts should work together, the OTP handwriting expert and an expert to be proposed by the Defence. The modus operandi should be simple enough. If this is studied in Belgrade, the diary or the note, then this protected witness should be called to provide a sample of his handwriting. The experts could then withdraw for an analysis of the original document. It's difficult to have a copy analysed because of the pressure applied when putting pen to paper and that sort of thing. The Trial Chamber is fully aware of all these things. So the first thing is authenticity. On the other hand, I think the Defence is right when saying that after all of this the handwriting should be analysed again. We have noticed that the sections proposed as singled out by the OTP must be considered as part of the overall context that stemmed from the examination-in-chief as well as the cross-examination, to check whether the witness provided truthful and legitimate answers. I don't think this should be a difficult matter to tackle since there is goodwill both on the part of the OTP and the Defence. Even as soon as next week would be a convenient time to study the diary. We have successfully deciphered our photocopy. I must inform the Chamber that we only received interpretations of portions of this diary, not the whole diary. Some of the paragraphs have not been translated at all, which the Defence believes to be extremely important. It is in relation to these untranslated passages that I've been successful in deciphering them since I can read the handwritings. There are a great many matters that I believe might be of interest to the Chamber as well. So we have this joint proposal, on the one hand, to have the document fully translated into English. That means including all the remaining passages that for the time being remain untranslated. That said, I believe we are entirely under on the right track, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We agree, Mr. Borovic, that in the circumstances it would be highly desirable for the two experts to work together. In the majority of cases, they reach a common mind, and if that's so, we can all proceed with confidence. And if you see a need for translation, you will have to arrange that or discuss it with Mr. Moore. I don't understand there to be need for any particular order for the diary to be provided at Belgrade. I think that has already been sufficiently ordered. Has it not, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, even if it wasn't, we would ensure that it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will leave that then for counsel to liaise and hopefully the matter can be clarified, and we'll get reports, if necessary, in due course. Now, Mr. Moore, there was any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to Witness 001, I've suggested that my learned friend Mr. Vasic had not put the case as disclosed by the summary. We checked that, and it is correct that that element of the case came by way of supplementary note. My learned friend was correct. We were not. I explained it to him last week and apologised, and I regret I did not inform the Court. It slipped my mind. My apologies for that. But I did speak to my learned friend about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're grateful for that, Mr. Moore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the only other matter was in relation to Mr. Sljivancanin's case, and I'm going to leave that to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. To gather strength before facing Mr. Lukic's submission, we will now just have a short break, perhaps five minutes. The tapes won't need to be changed because we can still finish, I expect, within the predicted time, but it will give everybody a chance to be refreshed. We adjourn for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we expect Mr. Vasic shortly? Very good. Now, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the break I asked Mr. Moore what the subject was that I was supposed to tackle in such an important manner. The two of us, however, have been talking during the previous break about the duration of my case, and I expect that the matter is of interest to the Chamber too. I would like to use this opportunity to raise another matter not related to this one. What I really like about Mr. Moore, and I think I should say that publicly, is he says, according to him, the time that I have envisaged for my witnesses is reasonable. Just to give you his position on that on the record. Last Friday, as I gave you the list to familiarise yourself with, the way in which I drew up the time schedule for Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence case, since the Chamber is now familiar with a great many persons and names from this list, I probably needn't even go into the nature of some of these witnesses. That is probably the case for most of these witnesses as far as the facts in this case are concerned. I've drawn your attention to the fact that some of these witnesses have provided very extensive statements to the OTP already, which only goes to show that the OTP seem to have had quite a number of issues to raise with these persons. Furthermore, many of these witnesses appeared in the Ovcara trial in Belgrade, some of them even on multiple occasions. And during the OTP case, the Chamber surely realised that this is a time-consuming exercise when the witnesses are confronted with statements and evidence from the Ovcara trial in Belgrade. Some of these witnesses we believe to be of exceptional interest to the other Defence teams as well. So when I thought about the cross-examination, I think two-thirds of the allotted time should go to the other Defence teams. We're still thinking about Rule 89. We've seen all these witnesses come and go very quickly these days. They speak about simple facts. We may have such witnesses. We may bring them here to testify, whereas we may drop some others. The crucial witnesses will take up the most of our time, including the appearance of Mr. Sljivancanin himself, and that is why the result is what it is in terms of our envisaged case duration. I'm open to any questions and any issues that need raising about this. That's one topic. The other topic, and probably Mr. Moore will have something to say about this, too, that is not related to this matter, but I would like to see what the Chamber's position is. You have already ruled on the right of the OTP to interview some of these 65 ter witnesses list -- some of the witnesses from the Defence 65 ter list. I know that some of these witnesses have already been summoned to the ICTY office in Belgrade to be interviewed over the following period. I asked Mr. Moore about your ruling, and he said he'd be informing me in due course and in good time about when they would be interviewing these witnesses. Nonetheless, there is one thing that I would like to know the Chamber's position on, just to see whether I'm wrong or whether I'm in fact on the right track. When I read your ruling, your decision, my understanding was that the right of the OTP to interview these witnesses arose out of the need for a rebuttal or re-examination of those witnesses. My interpretation of your decision was that this right for the OTP stemmed from the fact that the Defence were not serving on the OTP any witness statements, and we are not required to. So this was the only way for the OTP to find out about these circumstances, namely, by interviewing these witnesses. One specific witness, number 13 on my list, has so far given evidence before the security administration, before the military court, twice in the Ovcara trial. The transcripts of his testimony run into about 40 pages. Plus, in 2003 he was interviewed by the OTP, and the interview is about 50 pages long, plus another 50 if you take into account the translation, plus the audiotape, because the interview was recorded. And this was only in relation to matters relevant to this trial. They have now informed me that they wish to speak to this witness again. The thing is, I really believe that there is a possibility after so much evidence he has already provided the OTP wish to speak to him yet again. I understand the OTP's ambition, but I think the witnesses that can be interviewed are witnesses that the OTP knows nothing about, and the summaries may not be sufficient, and yet we have a position now, a situation where the OTP knows so much about a witness and yet they wish to talk to him yet again, and I think this opens an avenue for the OTP in the future to interview witnesses as many times as they like, whereas in relation to this particular witness they have literally truckloads of material to familiarise themselves with all the relevant matters that might be raised in cross-examination. I did not understand your ruling to be about that and to be to that effect; namely, entitling the OTP to talk to whoever they liked, especially in this case since they already have a number of different statements and lot of evidence from this witness. So much for the envisaged duration of our case, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were -- we were really hoping to learn from you a little more about the extent of your defence case, Mr. Lukic. In that respect, are you effectively saying, "We've pruned it as -- to as much a degree as we safely can, we have been conservative in the hours that we've allowed, and even Mr. Moore agrees"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Even, Mr. Moore. That's the high point of the strength of Mr. Lukic's submission, you see. Is that essentially what you're putting?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely my point, in essence. In relation to what was originally envisaged in terms of the duration of our case and the 65 ter list, we've been pruning the duration of all of our chiefs. If I were to start paring back even more, I would maybe place myself into a situation where I would be reprimanded by the Chamber, and I don't want to keep watching the time as I'm examining a witness. I do, however, believe that there are witnesses that will be appearing during our case that merit due attention, and that is what my estimate is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And so you effectively see yourself as perhaps needing 36 days, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly speaking, yes. I mean, if you're holding me to it, I would like to exercise the right that Mr. Moore mentioned at the Pre-Trial Conference. He said it would only take four months, his case, and yet it took a total of seven. Try as hard as I might to prune my case as Your Honour has suggested, I think this remains a realistic estimate. I'm not sure if the punishment imposed on me would be the same as that imposed on Mr. Moore, were my case to transcend the limits envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would like to record our appreciation of the efforts made by Defence counsel in reviewing their requirements to present their cases, and we are somewhat encouraged by the success of their efforts. Given the circumstances, the Chamber will really proceed upon the basis now advanced by the Defence without proposing to impose any greater restriction of witnesses or time. That being so, as we would see it, the case for Mr. Mrksic should finish by Friday -- no later than Friday, the 6th of October, which, as the way things are going, may allow you a little bit of spare room, Mr. Vasic. If it is spare, I know your friends would like to have it. So don't slow down, but you could run through until the 6th. On Mr. Borovic's estimate, that should mean that his case would conclude by Friday, the 20th of October, giving him his full measure. And Mr. Lukic would be Friday, the 8th of December, as we do a rough calculation of the time ahead, which hopefully will be the programme that we will be able to maintain. Mr. Vasic, the expert report mentioned by Mr. Moore, when do you think that is to be available?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, over the previous break I spoke to my learned friend, Mr. Moore, about this matter. The expert report was drafted and has been passed over to the translation service. I hope that the translation will be completed by the end of this week and that on Monday we can submit it to Mr. Moore. The expert report itself is not very lengthy, and I can therefore reassure Mr. Moore that in fact he will not need as much time as he thought. The B/C/S original version of the expert report has around 12 pages, and the English version will be thereabouts. I believe that this will enable Mr. Moore to review the report and respond to it within the set time-limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Vasic. That's, I think, helped with that. Could we mention two other matters in respect of timetable. As you know, a Plenary requires that the Chamber not sit tomorrow. There has been a further Plenary proposed by the President for Wednesday of next week, but it is one which this Chamber is able to avoid attending. So we will be able to sit next week according to the programme, and we will only attend the afternoon of the Plenary that day. Mr. Borovic's case, if all goes as we all hope, should finish by Friday, the 20th of October. The following Tuesday is United Nations Day and a holiday. It seemed that it might be to the advantage of everybody if we did not sit on the Monday. If that can be kept in mind, especially as Mr. Lukic plans his witness arrivals. We would then be able to have a longer weekend that weekend and commence evidence on the Wednesday. Now, Mr. Moore, that brings us to Mr. Lukic's other point. Can I say the Chamber is not usually in the position or the habit, and it is not appropriate for it to be explaining its decisions, and we won't. But if there is a current problem about one witness mentioned by Mr. Lukic, can you assist us with your position, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That won't quite do, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we abide by the ruling of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you wanting to interview this witness again, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Issues have arisen in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in light of the Court's ruling, we wish to interview him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there was a comment made by Mr. Lukic that you're summoning witnesses to be interviewed by you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is for a witness to come, it's not a summoning from this Court but it's required within the Serbian jurisdiction. It's nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I don't mean for witnesses to attend here but for you to speak to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. One has to arrange a specific date. My understanding is that you arrange a specific date and therefore that clarifies the date, and appointments are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is the way. It's not in any oppressive form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I take it from that you're not proceeding on the basis that the witnesses must give you a further statement if they decline to do so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. There's a second procedure that exists if needs be, but that's -- it's a matter for them. That is my understanding of the law. Although if I find a number of witnesses consistently doing it, one -- well, anyway. My understanding of the law is they are summoned. It is a matter for them whether they wish to give evidence or not, and if they do not, then other matters may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. It's a matter for them whether they wish to speak to you or not and give you further information or a further statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting you. I'd like to know what Mr. Moore's further position is in the event the witnesses refuse to participate in the interview. What follows next? That is what we'd like to know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to indicate your position, Mr. Moore, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will wait and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not aware, Mr. Borovic, of what Mr. Moore has in mind. In the understanding of the Chamber, if anything more was to happen, it would require the matter being brought before the Chamber, and then there is some nice questions. But I haven't studied that yet because we don't have an actual case before us. We do have an actual case, it seems, from Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there remains a motion by Defence affecting this issue which we are yet to determine, but subject to that, in the view of the Chamber the decision that it has given already would allow the Prosecution to seek to speak to any of the witnesses at this stage, whether it is for the first or a repeat time, and what the witness does about that is a matter for the witness. And in those circumstances, the Chamber is not at the moment minded to make any further or different order. Well, in view of the circumstances, as there appear to be no other loose ends about at the moment, we will now adjourn to resume on Thursday, at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
